summary: For ages 6–7 (Year 2): counting in tens from ANY number, not just multiples of ten (e.g. 7, 17, 27, 37…). The core place-value insight is that adding or subtracting 10 keeps the ones digit the same while the tens digit changes by one — and at a hundred boundary such as 96 → 106 the tens roll from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears (backwards, 106 → 96, they roll from 0 to 9), while the ones digit still does not move. This is the foundation for mental +10/−10 and later column place value. It is best made visible as a vertical move on a hundred square (on a standard square numbered from 1 at the top, straight down = +10 and straight up = −10; check the direction on squares numbered from the bottom), with concrete support from base-ten blocks (add/remove a ten-rod, ones untouched). Practise forwards and backwards from non-multiples and say the rule aloud.
misconceptions: Changing the ones digit too (e.g. 27 → 38) — not isolating the +10 to the tens.
Only able to add 10 to multiples of 10 (can't start from 7 or 23).
Treating +10 as 'just add a 0' — which fails for non-round numbers (27 ≠ 270).
Losing the column on the hundred square (drifting sideways instead of straight down).

activities.title: Down a column, ones frozen — the +10/−10 move on the hundred square
steps: Start on a non-multiple, e.g. 27, on a hundred square.
Make a +10 move by dropping straight DOWN one row: 27 → 37 → 47 → 57, saying each number aloud.
Each step of this 27 → 57 run, point to the ones digit (the 7) and say 'the ones stay the same'; point to the tens digit and say 'the tens go up by one' (true while you stay inside a hundred).
Reverse it: make −10 moves by going straight UP one row: 83 → 73 → 63 → 53, saying what stays (the ones) and what changes (the tens).
Watch for drifting sideways — keep the move strictly vertical so you stay in the same ones-digit column.
activities.insight: Adding or subtracting ten never touches the ones digit; it is the same single downward (or upward) step on the hundred square whatever number you start from. '+10' is not 'add a zero' — it is 'one row down'.

activities.title: Concrete why: add a ten-rod with base-ten blocks
steps: Build a two-digit number with base-ten blocks, e.g. 23 as two ten-rods and three ones.
To add 10, bring in ONE more ten-rod and leave the ones pile untouched; read the new number (33).
To subtract 10, take one ten-rod away and leave the ones pile untouched; read the new number.
Say the rule as you go: 'one more ten, the ones don't change'.
Link each action to its numeral and, if available, to the hundred-square move.
activities.insight: Physically, +10 is just one extra ten-rod; the ones stay as they are. This is the concrete reason the ones digit never changes.

activities.title: Say-it and spot-the-slip practice
steps: Answer quick questions: 'What is 10 more than 47?' and 'What is 10 less than 47?'
Fill in a tens sequence from a non-multiple, e.g. 4, 14, __, __, 44.
Look at a wrong sequence (e.g. 7, 17, 28, 38) and say which digit changed that shouldn't have.
Count aloud forwards from a non-multiple and backwards from a two-digit number, stating each step is +10 or −10.
activities.insight: Fluent +10/−10 from any starting number, with the ability to notice when the ones digit has wrongly moved.

activities.title: Explain the pattern out loud
steps: Count in tens from a non-multiple, then answer: 'What stays the same each time, and what changes?'
Answer in your own words why the ones digit stays the same each time and what happens to the tens.
Try harder prompts: ten less than 43 (33); ten more than 96 (106, crossing 100).
activities.insight: Being able to articulate that each step adds or removes one ten — so the ones digit always stays the same while the tens digit changes by one, rolling over into a new hundred at a boundary like 96 → 106 where the ones (6) still does not move — shows place-value reasoning rather than just the chant.

checkQuestion: Start at 7 and count on in tens: 7, 17, 27… keep going as far as you can. Now start at 83 and count backwards in tens. (Watch whether only the tens digit changes while the ones stays fixed, and whether they cross the hundred boundary cleanly.)
checkAnswer: 7, 17, 27, 37, …, 97, 107… and 83, 73, 63, …, 13, 3 — keeping the ones digit fixed and changing only the tens digit by one each step.
